newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt slackens, antimony stable in minor metals.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt slackens, antimony stable in minor metals.

text.p: Cobalt settled back slightly in the minor industrial metals market while antimony continued to edge away from depressed November levels, with reasonable activity seen ahead of the end-year holiday season.
Elsewhere, price levels were generally stable in metals such as magnesium, while pockets of activity in former laggards such as the depressed cadmium market helped values start to edge up.
"There is some business going on - nothing startling - but enough to suggest that some people still have spot stuff to book before the end of the year," one trader said.

In cobalt, Russian ingot prices were perhaps slightly lower, with a spot backwardation easing, while high grade cathode price levels remained steady against a background of good demand prospects in 1997.
"It is a little bit dull on the spot (Russian) market, because the number of people who have to buy is quite limited. On the high grade there is good long-term business," a trader said.
As always with cobalt, the market is keeping a cautious eye on developments in the African copperbelt, particularly in Zaire. So far, there appears to be no threat to supplies.
But the possibility of this will keep the market underpinned next year, when prices could appreciate considerably.
Russian cobalt business was reported around $21/lb, with prices slightly lower from a week ago levels. The backwardation narrowed to $0.10/0.40 from levels of $1.00 a month ago.

Meanwhile, the high grade market looks set to expand the premium over Russian. Better quality grades are in short supply already, and 1997 spot availability will be limited, as many producers are fully committed.
The differential between high grade and Russian is currently some $2.00, but has been as small as $0.50 earlier this year.
In antimony, business centred on the $2,150/2,175 a tonne area, with prices now well established above the sub-$2,000 levels of last month.
Traders said the market was helped by a lack of Chinese offers over the last two weeks, although some material is now being made available around $2,150/tonne.

As production is unprofitable at levels of $2,000/tonne, not only in China but elsewhere, signs of offers drying up suggests that the market has seen its floor for now. However, the upside is unlikely to be dramatic in the short-term, as the general level of business is still low-key.
Cadmium prices were moving up from depressed mid-November levels, with a cheap market having attracted demand from the Far East and India.
Prices for "four-nines" ingots were some 10 cents above a recent floor of $0.75, while "three-nine-fives" sticks were a similar margin up from a recent low around $0.68.
Magnesium prices were slightly steadier, with Chinese metal transacted around the $2,550/tonne level, while CIS material was being booked at some $2,650/tonne.
Elsewhere, ferro-tungsten prices showed signs of pushing up from depressed levels as well, as the excess material in the market which emanated from Eastern stockpiles has dried up.
